blocks.text: Feature Extraction, earlier in this module, briefly covered simple text statistics, word count, character count, a sentiment score. Text Features goes considerably deeper into that same raw material, covering the genuine preprocessing steps that come first, and the classic techniques, bag of words and TF-IDF, that turn free form text into a genuinely rich, structured numeric representation a model can actually learn from.

This topic covers the standard text preprocessing pipeline, the bag of words representation and its real limitations, TF-IDF weighting and why it genuinely improves on plain word counts, n-grams for capturing a bit of word order, the real vocabulary size problem that comes with text data, and a brief preview of word embeddings as the modern, automated alternative to all of these manual techniques.
1. Preprocessing Text Before Extracting Anything

blocks.alt: Raw text is lowercased into clean tokens

blocks.text: Raw text genuinely needs cleaning before most extraction techniques work well. Lowercasing treats Great and great as the genuinely same word, rather than two different ones. Removing punctuation strips out genuine noise, commas and periods that carry little useful signal on their own. Removing stopwords drops extremely common words like the and is, which appear constantly across almost every document and rarely help distinguish one from another.

Stemming or lemmatization goes one step further, genuinely reducing running, ran, and runs down to a single common root, run, so that a model treats them as expressions of the genuinely same underlying concept rather than as unrelated words.
2. The Bag of Words Representation

blocks.alt: A sentence becomes word counts, then a vector

blocks.text: Bag of words builds a genuine vocabulary of every unique word appearing across a whole collection of documents, and represents each individual document as a count of how many times each vocabulary word appears in it. The word order is genuinely discarded entirely, a document is treated as an unordered bag of words, hence the name.

This is a genuinely simple, surprisingly effective starting point, turning free form text of any length into a fixed size numeric vector a classical machine learning algorithm can directly consume, exactly filling the gap left open by the Unstructured Data topic much earlier in this course.
3. TF-IDF: Weighting Words by How Distinctive They Are

blocks.alt: A common word gets a low weight while a rare, distinctive word gets a high weight

blocks.text: Plain word counts have a genuine weakness, a word appearing in almost every single document, even after removing common stopwords, tells you genuinely little about what makes any one document distinctive. TF-IDF, short for term frequency inverse document frequency, fixes this directly, giving a genuinely low weight to words that appear in nearly every document, and a genuinely high weight to words that appear often in one document but rarely across the rest of the collection.

A word like screen might appear reasonably often across many product reviews, earning a moderate weight, while a genuinely distinctive word like cracked, appearing in only a handful of reviews, earns a genuinely higher, more informative weight under TF-IDF, exactly the kind of signal plain word counts alone would treat as equally important as any other word.

blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example
Computing TF-IDF with scikit-learn shows the genuine weighting effect directly, applied to a small set of product reviews.

code.content:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

reviews = [
    "Great battery life, would buy again.",
    "Screen cracked after one week, very disappointed.",
    "Great screen, but battery life is short.",
]

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(reviews)

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(tfidf_matrix.toarray())

blocks.text: Words like great and battery, appearing across more than one review, end up with a genuinely lower weight than a word like cracked or disappointed, which appears in only one review and stands out as genuinely distinctive to it, exactly the behavior TF-IDF is designed to produce.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always preprocess text, lowercasing, removing punctuation and stopwords, before running TfidfVectorizer. Skipping this step lets uninformative variation, like capitalization differences, quietly inflate the vocabulary for no real benefit.

blocks.text: 5. N-Grams: Recovering a Bit of Word Order

blocks.alt: Single words become word pairs, capturing some order

blocks.text: Bag of words and TF-IDF both genuinely discard word order entirely, which creates a real problem for phrases where order changes meaning, not good and good not are treated as identical under a pure single word, or unigram, approach, even though they mean genuinely opposite things. N-grams address this directly, treating pairs or triples of consecutive words, bigrams and trigrams, as their own vocabulary entries alongside single words.

Adding bigrams lets not good genuinely register as its own distinct feature, separate from the individual words not and good, recovering a meaningful piece of the word order information that a pure unigram approach loses entirely.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Adding bigrams and trigrams genuinely helps capture short, meaningful phrases, but it also genuinely multiplies the vocabulary size considerably, directly feeding into the vocabulary explosion problem covered next.

blocks.text: 6. The Real Vocabulary Size Problem

blocks.alt: Many documents together produce a huge vocabulary

blocks.text: A genuinely small, curated vocabulary produces a manageable number of features, but real text collections routinely contain thousands of unique words, and adding bigrams multiplies that count considerably further. The result is a genuinely large, sparse matrix, mostly zeros, since any single document only ever uses a small fraction of the full vocabulary.

This is a direct, specific instance of the same high dimensional challenge first previewed back in Multivariate Analysis and covered fully in the existing Curse of Dimensionality topic, text data is genuinely one of the most common real sources of that exact problem, which is precisely why the Dimensionality Reduction and Feature Selection modules later in this course matter so directly for text heavy projects.

blocks.text: 7. Word Embeddings: A Brief Preview of the Automated Path

blocks.alt: A word maps to a dense embedding vector

blocks.text: Every technique covered so far in this topic is genuinely manual and rule based, exactly the manual side of the manual versus automated distinction first introduced in the Feature Extraction topic. Word embeddings represent the automated side for text specifically, a pretrained model converts each word, or even an entire document, into a dense numeric vector that genuinely captures meaning, not just presence or frequency.

Under embeddings, words with genuinely similar meaning end up with genuinely similar numeric vectors, even if they never actually appear together in the same document, a capability plain bag of words or TF-IDF simply cannot offer. This is only a brief preview here, the full technique sits outside the manual scope of this topic, but it is worth knowing this more powerful, automated alternative genuinely exists.
8. Text Features Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Text features are covered here, aggregation features come next

blocks.text: This topic pushed the basic text extraction from earlier in this module considerably further, proper preprocessing, bag of words, TF-IDF weighting, n-grams, and a preview of the more advanced embeddings alternative. Together with Date Features, the previous topic, this rounds out a genuinely deep treatment of the two major unstructured forms first introduced back in the Data Collection and Understanding module.

The next topic, Aggregation Features, shifts direction once again, moving away from extracting signal out of a single row content, whether text, dates, or otherwise, toward summarizing information across entire groups of related rows instead.

items: Text preprocessing, lowercasing, removing punctuation and stopwords, and stemming, comes before extraction.
Bag of words represents text as word counts, discarding word order entirely.
TF-IDF weights words by how distinctive they are to one document versus the whole collection.
N-grams, like bigrams, recover a bit of word order information that plain bag of words loses.
Text data is a common, real source of the vocabulary size explosion behind the curse of dimensionality.
Word embeddings offer a more powerful, automated alternative to these manual, rule based techniques.
